text.p: Zinc raced ahead in London on waves of speculative buying on Friday, sweeping aluminium, copper and nickel with it.
Gold, wheat and oil also firmed in U.S. trading, helping to push up the Commodity Research Bureau Index by 0.74 points to 238.48.
Zinc galloped higher on Friday afternoon on waves of speculative buying, sweeping other key metals with it in hectic trading on the London Metal Exchange.

"Once one metal gets going, the euphoria tends to spill over," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis hree months zinc touched a seven-year peak of $1,625 per tonne, bringing gains over the past two days to $100 and the month's rise to $204 or 14 percent. It ended the day $53 higher at $1,624.
The relentless rally has been fuelled by a battle between short Chinese smelters and long speculators.
The Chinese sold heavily short as much as 250,000 tonnes at low prices last year, analysts said.
Funds who expected a correction after prices hit $1,500 scrambled to cover short positions and have gone long, while delta hedging by option grantors has also fuelled the rise.

Option buyers have been snapping up both upside calls and downside puts, to profit from any further gains, but fearful that overcharged conditions may be building up for a breathless tumble. Analysts on Friday held out prospects that prices could sustain momentum to $1,700 and one said they may revisit $2,000, which prices last hit in March 1989.
The tightness, centred in September, forced the premium of cash over three months up about $20 to $60 at one point, ending the day at $55.
After zinc broke up through $1,600 in the afternoon, the U.S. funds piled into the other metals in a hectic LME session.

Aluminium also scored more upside gains, climbing $31 to a peak of $1,691, the highest since March 7. The next target was the $1,701 high on March 4, which is also the peak for the year so far. The key for the market would be whether producers decide to start selling heavily, Bahr said.
Nickel charged up on furious short-covering, adding $405 in the space of a couple of hours to end at its high of $7,180.
Worries over contract talks which broke down at producer Falconbridge underpinned the rise. The current contract covering 1,400 workers at the Sudbury operation expires end July.
Copper also joined in the fray, adding $82 to $2,374.
But once the short-covering was done, there was not a lot of scope for further gains as stocks keep growing, analysts said.
COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended higher across the board Friday on moderate volumes with nearby active September palladium registering a new contract high.
"Gold and silver are choppy, with influential speculators going long in the morning and taking profits in the afternoon this week," PaineWebber analyst Bernard Savaiko said.
"Gold may still be oversold, but the question is where is it going to go on the upside with stocks, bonds and dollar still strong," he said.
COMEX August gold ended up $2.70 an ounce at $326.50, after trading a $323.50-328.00 range, compared with Thursday's range of $321.20-329.70.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $325.75/25, compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $324.10 and the New York close Thursday around $324.50/00.

Gold prices have been consolidating in the past two weeks after hitting a 12 year low in early July around $314.00 an ounce, following confirmation of a sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the Australian central bank.

NYMEX gasoline rallied on tightening supply due to high demand and the rising price of a key gasoline blending component, helping to push up the rest of the oil complex. September crude firmed 12 cents to $19.89 a barrel. August gasoline settled 1.82 cents higher at 64.03 cents a gallon.

CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed mostly firm on the potential for sales of U.S. wheat to Egypt and Pakistan, traders said. Wheat rallied early this week on news Egypt bought U.S. wheat and there was talk Egypt this weekend may purchase another 500,000 to one million tonnes. Wheat closed one cent higher to two cents lower, with September unchanged at $3.58-1/2.

CSCE world sugar futures closed firmer but off the new lifetime highs made across the board amid early mixed buying. Trade buying on the open carried second-position March to a high of 11.90 cents. The benchmark October contract settled 0.07 cent higher at 11.63 cents a lb, having ranged from 11.70 to 11.55 cents.
